newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany set to bolster role in Middle East peace.
newsitem.headline: Germany set to bolster role in Middle East peace.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel sets off on Tuesday for talks with top officials in Jordan, Gaza and Israel, determined to bolster his country's role in the floundering Middle East peace process.
Kinkel will aim to stress Germany's "particular commitment" to the peace process amid rising tension over Israel's decision to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
The European Union has deplored the move, saying "settlements in the occupied territories contravene international law and are a major obstacle to peace".

Germany, assuming a more active international role since its unification in 1990, has been hard at work trying to foster peace and economic development in the Middle East and is keen its efforts are not over-shadowed by France, also eager to carve out a key position in the region alongside the United States.
But the Foreign Ministry said Germany did not want to work against or be a competitor to its European Union (EU) partners or the United States in the region.
"It is important for us to co-operate and share tasks, not to be one-sided or interfere where we are not asked to," Kinkel's ministry said in a statement.
In contrast to France, whose President Jacques Chirac made a tumultuous tour to the Middle East last October, Germany has fostered a more "behind the scenes" approach in the region.

The country gained international acclaim last July when it brokered a deal between Lebanon's Hezbollah (Party of God) and Israel for Hezbollah's handover of the remains of two Israeli soldiers -- held for a decade -- in return for Arab prisoners and guerrilla remains held by the Jewish state.

Kinkel last visited the region exactly a year ago when he held talks with former Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, then PLO leader, after a spate of suicide bombings by Palestinian extremists.
Kinkel was due to meet top officials in Amman, Jericho, Jerusalem, Gaza and Tel Aviv in his four day trip.
He arrives in Jordan on Tuesday to hold talks with King Hussein and Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.
The Foreign Ministry described relations with Jordan as "friendly" and said King Hussein called Germany the most important European partner in the peace process when he visited Bonn last month.
Kinkel is likely to focus on the issue of water rights in the region, often a sticking point in talks with Israel.
He is expected to meet Arafat in Gaza on Thursday. The Palestinian President is currently visiting the United States.
The ministry said aid to Palestinians was at the core of Germany's support for peace in the region. It is the biggest EU donor and gave 40 million marks ($23.6 million) in direct aid in 1996.
Kinkel will end his trip on Friday in Tel Aviv and meet President Ezer Weizman and Foreign Minister David Levy.
"Thanks to state and private committment, in most areas Germany has become Israel's second most important foreign partner (after the United States)," the ministry said.

Germany and Israel have in recent years put aside their painful past to form an unlikely friendship, but Bonn has said its support for Israel depends on continued efforts to push ahead with the peace process.

The Foreign Ministry said the stagnation in the peace process prompted by the wave of bombings early last year and the beginning of the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seemed to have ended for the moment.

"The danger of its complete failure has been temporarily averted," said the ministry. "It is now time to strengthen dynamism and positive foundations and encourage compromise." ($ = 1.694 German Marks)
